title: Scaling joint Kolmogorov-complexity profiles
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\) and real \(\lambda >0\), does there exist a constant \(c>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every tuple of binary strings \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}\) of length at most n, there are finite binary strings \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{k}\) satisfying |\(C(b_{S})- \lambda  C(a_{S})|\le c \log _{2} n\) for every nonempty \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,k\}\)? The same tuple b must satisfy all \(2^{k}- 1\) inequalities simultaneously.
context:
Scaling each component separately can destroy its shared-information pattern with other components. The target scales the entire joint profile, retaining those dependencies.

The original card asked for \(\lambda =1/2\). The retained question asks for every fixed positive \(\lambda\), as in Question 1 of the 2025 paper. It is a broader formulation; no equivalence to the single halving case is asserted.

The 2025 paper separates freely choosing a new tuple from conditioning the original tuple on one auxiliary string. Its negative conditioning result does not settle the new-tuple problem. Its discussion retains nonintegral scaling for general tuples as open.
why: Scaling complete algorithmic-information profiles asks whether shared information has a universal homogeneous geometry, across arbitrary tuples rather than one example.
status_note: The 2025 primary source retains the general scaling question; its conditioning obstruction is a different target.

sentences: Every tuple of strings has a profile of complexities of its nonempty subtuples.
The question asks whether that whole profile can be multiplied by any fixed positive real factor.
One new tuple must realize all the scaled quantities within logarithmic additive error.
No fixed algorithm mapping the old tuple to the new one is required.
The target concerns the homogeneous geometry of shared algorithmic information.

definitions: Fix one optimal plain Kolmogorov machine U: an optimal partial computable map from finite binary programs to finite binary strings. \(C(x)\) is the minimum program length with U(program)=x. For \(S=\{i_{1}<\cdots <i_{r}\}\), encode the tuple \(x_{S}\) as \(1^{r}0\) followed, in that order, by the strings \(1^{|x_{i}|}0x_{i}\), and let \(C(x_{S})\) mean the complexity of this encoding. This is a fixed computably decodable encoding. The strings \(b_{i}\) have no prescribed lengths and need not be computable from the \(a_{i}\) by a fixed transformation. Only joint unconditional complexities of all nonempty subtuples are required. The constants may depend on \(k, \lambda\) and U but not on n, the input strings or S. The additive slack is measured in bits. This uses the original length normalization \(O(\log  n)\); it does not silently replace it by the potentially smaller \(O(\log  C(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}))\).
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal statement, or its logical negation with the same quantifier order. Failure of one algorithm for producing b, or failure of obtaining the scaling by conditioning the original strings on an auxiliary string, is not a refutation. The logarithmic slack is part of the proposition, not a numerical-estimation tolerance.
